newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK OFT slams pension industry shortcomings.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK OFT slams pension industry shortcomings.

text.p: Millions of Britons are losing out because of shortcomings in pension products, according to a hard-hitting report from the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) published on Tuesday.
Director General of Fair Trading John Bridgeman called for radical changes in attitude and provision if consumer interests were to be adequately safeguarded.

He attacked the performance of fund managers, calling on government ministers to incorporate in future pensions policy a new passively managed product -- one which tracks market performance rather than trying to achieve better returns by active selection of investments.
Existing pension products, he said, were marketed in an unnecessarily complex way, emphasising superior investment performance which Bridgeman described as "insubstantial and illusory".
"There is no convincing evidence that fund managers can consistently outperform the market over the period of a pension plan although the industry does not like to face up to this," he said.
The OFT criticised personal pension plans for providing poor value with benefits frequently being eroded by the high cost of marketing and fund management.
While it said that occupational pensions might have improved in recent years, those who left early -- as the majority do -- lost out.

Today's report comes at a bad time for the beleagured pensions industry, already reeling from heavy criticisms of its handling of the pensions misselling scandal of the late 1980s and early 1990s when as many as 1-1/2 million people may have been wrongly advised to opt out of occupational schemes.
Later this week the government is expected to launch its own wide-ranging review of pensions provision.

The OFT's proposed new pension product -- the designated personal pension (DPP) -- would be a portable, passively managed 'defined contribution' scheme and would need to be adequately funded, where appropriate, by the employer, said Bridgeman.
It would not penalise those who changed jobs and would not have to bear heavy fund management and distribution costs.
Wide provision should be encouraged by changes to the tax system, said Bridgeman but he drew back from calling for it to be mandatory.
Alongside existing providers, the OFT envisaged alternative channels for the DPP, such as building socities or unions.
The DPP would employ a tracker fund which shadows stock market performance, doing away with the higher costs associated with active fund management.
It would be designed to provide more flexible pension arrangements and encourage those falling through the pensions net to take out provision.
Around 25 percent of the workforce have no pension provision and some 45 percent of the population will rely on the state for income unless adequate provision is made.

The OFT inquiry, launched in September 1996, attacked the way expenses of personal pension plans were often loaded onto the early years of the plan and weighed disproportionately on those discontinuing the pension.
Employers' contributions were also often inadequate or non-existent, it added.

The report also highlighted that employees in occupational pension schemes who moved employers several times could find their occupational pension up to 30 percent lower than someone who stayed in the same scheme.
The pension rights that employees received on leaving 'defined benefit' schemes were also subject to a large degree of actuarial discretion which could dramatically reduce their size.
Problems with defined contribution schemes arose from inefficient and expensive selling methods and costly fund management.
Many contribution levels were inadequate and people had unwarranted optimism in what they would get at the end of it, the report said.
"People contribute to their pension for 40 years and only then do they find out what they've bought," said Bridgeman.
